body.objective: Students will be able to explain neurons and brain structures.
body.iCan: I can explain neurons and brain structures.
successCriteria: I can describe the parts of a neuron and how it sends a message
I can name major brain structures and their functions
I can explain how neurotransmitters work at the synapse
body.hook: Right now, about 86 billion neurons in your brain are firing electrical and chemical signals so you can read this sentence. Every thought, memory and movement you have is built from these tiny messages.

vocabulary.definition: A nerve cell that sends electrical and chemical messages.
Branches of a neuron that receive messages.
The long fibre that carries a message away from the cell body.
The tiny gap between neurons where messages are passed chemically.
A chemical messenger released into the synapse.
The wrinkled outer layer of the brain responsible for thinking, planning and language.
The four main regions of the cortex: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital.

study.title: Message in the Brain
study.question: How does the nervous system send messages, and what do brain structures do?
study.passage:
The neuron: Messages arrive at the dendrites, travel through the cell body, then down the axon as an electrical impulse (action potential). The myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds the signal. At the axon terminals, neurotransmitters are released into the synapse and bind to receptors on the next neuron.
Key neurotransmitters: dopamine (reward and movement), serotonin (mood, sleep), acetylcholine (muscle movement, memory), endorphins (pain relief).
Brain structures: frontal lobe (planning, decisions, personality; still developing into the mid-20s), parietal lobe (touch, spatial awareness), temporal lobe (hearing, language comprehension, memory), occipital lobe (vision), cerebellum (balance and coordination), brainstem (breathing, heart rate), limbic system including the amygdala (fear, emotion) and hippocampus (forming memories).
Case: Phineas Gage (1848), a railway worker, survived an iron rod passing through his frontal lobe. Friends said he was "no longer Gage": more impulsive and less reliable. His case showed the frontal lobe's role in personality.
Activity: Human neuron chain. Students act as dendrites, cell body, axon and terminals; pass a "signal" (squeeze) down the chain. Then build a labelled brain map.

practice.a: A nerve cell that sends messages.

practice.q: What does the myelin sheath do?
practice.a: Insulates the axon and speeds signals.

practice.q: What is the function of the frontal lobe?
Why was Phineas Gage important to psychology?
practice.a: His case linked the frontal lobe to personality and self-control.

practice.q: Why might teens take more risks?
practice.a: The frontal lobe, which controls impulses, is still developing.

practice.q: How do some medications for depression work?
practice.a: They affect levels of neurotransmitters like serotonin.

practice.q: Why is the brainstem essential for life?
practice.a: It controls breathing and heart rate.

items.q: A neuron is
items.answer: A) a nerve cell

items.q: Dendrites
items.answer: B) receive messages

items.q: The synapse is
items.answer: A) the gap between neurons

items.q: The occipital lobe processes
items.answer: A) vision

items.q: Myelin
options: C) speeds signals along the axon
items.answer: C) speeds signals along the axon

items.q: The hippocampus helps
items.answer: A) form new memories

items.q: Dopamine is linked to
items.answer: C) reward and movement

items.q: The cerebellum controls
items.answer: C) balance and coordination

items.q: The order of a message through a neuron is
options: A) dendrites, cell body, axon, terminals
B) terminals, axon, cell body, dendrites
C) cell body, dendrites, terminals, axon
D) axon, dendrites, terminals, cell body
items.answer: A) dendrites, cell body, axon, terminals

items.q: Phineas Gage's injury showed the frontal lobe affects
items.answer: D) personality and impulse control

items.q: Teens may take more risks because
options: B) the occipital lobe is too big
C) the frontal lobe is still developing
items.answer: C) the frontal lobe is still developing

items.q: The claim that we use only 10% of our brains is
items.answer: A) a myth

items.q: Define neurotransmitter.
items.answer: A chemical messenger released into the synapse.

items.q: What is the cerebral cortex?
items.answer: The brain's wrinkled outer layer for thinking and language.

items.q: Describe how a message travels from one neuron to the next.
items.answer: Electrical impulse down the axon, neurotransmitters cross the synapse, bind to receptors on the next neuron.

items.q: Name the four lobes and one function each.
items.answer: Frontal planning, parietal touch, temporal hearing, occipital vision.

items.q: What do the amygdala and hippocampus do?
items.answer: Amygdala: fear and emotion; hippocampus: forming memories.

items.q: Name two neurotransmitters and their roles.
items.answer: Answers vary.

items.q: Explain what the Phineas Gage case taught psychologists.
items.answer: The frontal lobe is involved in personality and self-control.

items.q: Explain how frontal lobe development relates to teen decision-making.
items.answer: It is still maturing, so impulse control and planning are still developing.
